title: How Aerosol Cans Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain how aerosol cans work, starting with the fluid dynamics basics: fluids, boiling at lower temperatures for volatile fluids, and gas expanding while losing pressure. They describe the two main designs: compressed-gas cans and liquefied-propellant cans, including the valve, dip tube, and how the nozzle atomizes product. They cover why cans have ball bearings for paint, why bottoms are domed, and aerosol history (Eric Rothheim's Norwegian patent, WWII insecticide bombs). They then discuss CFCs replacing ammonia in refrigeration, their role as aerosol propellants, ozone depletion from chlorine, and the phase-out treaties. The episode closes with a listener mail story from Terry Bennett about a 1980s bank robbery and FBI composite sketch, followed by a sign-off.

segments.title: Opening banter and aerosol can introduction
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck banter about the episode, then introduce aerosol cans and the Style Wars documentary, linking graffiti culture to the invention of the aerosol can.

segments.title: Eric Rothheim and aerosol history
segments.summary: Norwegian engineer Eric Rothheim filed the first aerosol can patent in Norway, then in the US five years later. Its value was slow to be recognized until insecticide bombs were used by soldiers in the Pacific in World War Two.

segments.title: Atomizing and basic fluid dynamics
segments.summary: The hosts explain the benefits of atomizing product into a fine mist, then define fluids, the fixed volume of liquids versus expanding gases, boiling as breaking intermolecular bonds, and volatile fluids boiling at lower temperatures.

segments.title: Gas pressure and compressed air
segments.summary: Gas loses pressure as it expands, and compressed gas can drive objects, as in CO2 cartridge Pinewood-style racers. Chuck shares a story about a high school race.

segments.title: How compressed-gas and liquefied-gas aerosol cans work
segments.summary: An aerosol can holds product and propellant. In the simpler design, compressed air pushes product up a dip tube through a spring-loaded valve when the nozzle is pressed. In the more common design, liquefied gas propellant mixes with the product under pressure and evaporates as it leaves, atomizing the product. Shaking mixes the contents.

segments.title: Domed can bottoms and product variety
segments.summary: The rounded bottom of a can resists pressure structurally and lets the product collect at the tube's opening so it can be fully emptied. Different products such as foam, whipped cream, and hair spray are produced by varying propellant ratio, chemistry, pressure, and valve design. Aerosol can recycling figures are mentioned.

segments.title: CFCs, refrigeration, and the ozone layer
segments.summary: Ammonia refrigerant leaks led to the development of CFCs, which DuPont turned into Freon. CFCs were used as aerosol propellants until scientists found in 1974 that they damaged the ozone layer, and a hole over the Arctic was found in the 1980s. Countries signed treaties to phase out CFC production. CFCs remain in some nasal sprays and halon fire extinguishers.

segments.title: Closing remarks on aerosols and graffiti
segments.summary: The hosts wrap up the aerosol topic, joking about graffiti and suggesting listeners search the HowStuffWorks site for more on aerosols.

segments.title: Listener mail: police sketch witness story
segments.summary: Listener Terry Bennett recounts being a bank teller during a robbery in the 1980s, working with an FBI sketch artist using feature transparencies, and the robber being caught at a methadone clinic using the composite sketch.

segments.summary: Hosts invite listener stories by Twitter, Facebook, email, and the website, and note the sponsor credit.
